The containment-breach RCA is done and clean. Root cause: the orchestrator reaps a pipeline-worker on the SAME edge that creates the worker's cascade work — 'pipeline row is terminal' means both 'there is cascade work to do' and 'this worker is no longer wanted'. 25909's worker was SIGTERMed 1.3s into its sweep and never respawned. **A — two smalls now, file the large.** (1) One predicate change: desiredSeqs becomes 'any non-terminal node in the subtree' instead of 'the root row is non-terminal'. Makes the reap honest, respawns a worker that dies mid-cascade, and auto-heals the existing 7-pipeline / 374-step residue on the next reconcile. **B — go large now.** Cascade terminal status atomically at the plpgsql write boundary and declare a coherenceRule making 'non-terminal child under terminal parent' unrepresentable, then delete the worker's cascade arms as dead code. This is the Existence-Check answer — it removes the deferred second writer entirely rather than keeping it alive. But it is large, on the hot page-write path, needs FizzBee coverage and a one-off repair, while we are bringing the fleet back up.

My read: A. Not because B is wrong — B is the principled endpoint and I would file it immediately as its own row — but because a plpgsql change on the page write boundary is the least appealing thing to land during a restart, and A closes the actual breach tonight at small cost.

Ignore the one-word "probe" just before this — mine, testing the address, and it should not have reached you.

Agreed on the body-shape split, and the machinery is further along than either of us thought.

**The seam is already named.** `page-check.ts`'s own help splits them in two capitalised sentences: "THE PAGE TYPE'S BODY IS THE SHAPE" and "WHAT THE FRONTMATTER ADDS IS THE BOUNDS." Two things living in one document, already described apart.

**The sharing is not speculative — it is already owed.** I hashed all 34 page type bodies. Fifteen distinct non-empty shapes; thirteen bodies empty. Two templates are each written three times: `email-rule-agent`, `category-rule-agent` and `turn-end-rule-agent` are byte-identical, and so are the three `-code` twins. Four documents of pure copy standing today.

**One correction to the plan.** Those six are identical in body and not in frontmatter. The `-agent` triple differ in exactly two slot value-lists — `field.values` and `test.values` — and agree on every bound. So the shape document should take the template and the shared bounds, and the page type keeps only what it narrows. `narrows:` already exists and is gated: `page-shape.ts` refuses a redeclaration that does not name what it narrows. There is already a home for the per-kind part.

**A prize you may not have counted.** `page-frontmatter.ts:141` reads "the registry levies no reading on its own files" — page type documents are exempt from shape checking today. That is the real reason the template body passes, not just the body slot being occupied. Move the template out and the 34 page types stop being exempt and become ordinary domain documents held to the domain shape. The exemption shrinks to fifteen shape documents.

**The one thing that gets harder, and my call on it.** `extends-id` is one key doing two jobs: `propertiesFor` and `shapeOf` both call the same `chainOf`. Split the shape out and there are two inheritances — properties up the page type chain, shape up the shape chain. I would give the shape document its own chain rather than derive it from the page type's. Deriving means two page types can share a shape only where they share ancestry, and the six that want to share share nothing: email, category and turn-end rules all extend `page` separately. Derivation kills the case that motivates the whole move.

**Earlier census, for the record.** Thirteen page types extend `domain` today, and they are exactly the thirteen whose `files:` glob points inside `domains/` — no exceptions. Separately, nineteen of the thirty-one name-sharing pairs write the same glob twice, once as `files:` on the page type and once as `instructions-path:` or `memory-path:` on the domain. `role` is the one pair writing two different globs under keys that read alike. Merging the pair puts that duplication into one frontmatter where it can be settled.

Next I draft the actual lines — the `page-body-shape` page type, and `page-type` getting its Definition back as a domain — and bring them to you one at a time, since these are Definition, Design and Intent lines.

**No worktree. There is no broken intermediate once it is sequenced.**

The thing that dissolves it is one line of ordering: teach `shapeOf` to read the shape key IF PRESENT and fall back to the body otherwise. That single fallback makes every later step independently green, and it is the difference between one big-bang merge and thirty small ones you can watch land.

**The path.**

A. Land `page-body-shape` as a page type, its properties, and `body-shape-id` on `page-type`. Then the fallback branch in `page-shape.ts`. All additive; nothing reads the new key yet; every check stays green.

B. Move one page type's template out, one kind at a time. Create the shape document, empty the page type's body, set `body-shape-id`. `pages-hold-shape` re-runs each time and holds that kind's pages to the same shape as before. Fifteen distinct shapes, and the six rule kinds collapse onto two of them — that is where the four duplicate documents die, visibly, mid-sequence.

C. Merge each domain twin into its page type, one kind at a time. `page-types/finding.md` gains `domain-slug`, `domain-parents` and the prose; `domains/finding.md` goes, in the same commit. `domain-edges.ts` refuses `domain-slug-declared-twice`, so the delete and the create have to travel together — which is what makes each of the thirty-one a small green commit rather than a window where the corpus contradicts itself. The body is prose by now, and passes, because `page-type` still declares no blocks. B must precede C for that reason and no other.

D. `page-types/page-type.md` takes `extends-id: <domain>`. One line. `page-check` goes from one declared part to sixteen for all 34, and they all already conform because of C. If C is incomplete this goes red immediately and by name, which is the check earning its place.

E. Remove the carve-out at `page-frontmatter.ts:142`. The reading it levies is now the domain chain.

F. Settle `files:` against `instructions-path:`/`memory-path:`, now that both stand in one frontmatter per kind. Nineteen kinds state one fact twice; `role` states two facts under keys that read alike.

**Why not the worktree, specifically.**

This repo is the harness. `Fast Correction` holds that a change here reaches every seat on the commit, and that speed is what makes a fault cheap to correct. A worktree merged as one commit reaches every seat at once with nothing measured in between — it converts a cheap fault into an expensive one.

`Composed Outside` applies to a worktree exactly as it applies here: a shell write into a gated repo is live the moment it lands and cannot be committed. The worktree does not buy a place to write freely, it moves where the gate refuses you.

And the checks are the proof of every step. Batching means one measurement at the end over thirty-odd moves nobody watched. Step B failing on the seventh kind is a fact worth having at the seventh kind.

The one thing a worktree genuinely buys is atomicity across a broken middle, and the fallback in A means there is no broken middle to cross.

C is thirty-one commits over the whole corpus. `Horizontal Change` says I land that myself in one run rather than dispatching it — one run, not one commit — so that is mine and I would take it in one sitting.

Say go and I start at A.

**Step B is done.** Twenty shape documents under `page-body-shapes/`, and every page type but three now names the shape its pages hold to. I spot-checked one page of each kind: domain 16 parts, role 18, task 23, persona 20, list 18, alert 16, notice 4, refusal 2, subagent 9, merchants 2, and the rule kinds 2 for code and 5 for agent. Those counts match what stood before the move, which is the proof the shapes are being read rather than silently emptied.

**A correction, and it revises what I promised you about sharing.** I said the six rule kinds would share a template and each narrow its own slot values. They cannot. I proved it rather than reasoned it — a child shape declaring `slots.field.values` over a parent's section is ignored outright, the compiled hole keeping the parent's values. Slot bounds bake into a section at the level whose template line carries it, so a child adding no section has nowhere to put a bound.

What saved the idea was reading the six properly. `email-rule-code` and `email-rule-agent` carry the same field vocabulary and the same match template; the agent one simply adds a `# Rule` section with an act and a description. So the family runs on the subject axis, not the agent/code axis: an agent rule's shape is a code rule's shape plus its judgment. Three parents, three children adding a section each, and the match template with its field lists written once per subject instead of twice. Real sharing, on an axis I had not seen.

**One forced batch.** Nine page types inherited `domain`'s template through `extends-id` and carried no body of their own. The moment `domain` stopped carrying the template they had nothing, so those nine and `domain` and the four that add to it went in one commit — fourteen files. **Two reds I did not touch, and why.** Two tests about ISO 8601 instants fail. I checked out the commit before my first one in a throwaway worktree and ran them there: they failed identically, so they are not mine and I left them. Separately the turn-end and headless-halt suites are failing and moving — another seat has four commits in this window against `turn-end-decide.ts` and `block-headless-halt.sh`, the failure count changed between two of my runs, and neither file references the shape machinery at all. Counting files that carry each declaration one of our checks parses, the branch against main:

- `predicate-derivation:` — 312 files on main, 0 on the branch. Each one held a hand-written warrant for why a predicate's set of spellings is closed or only sampled, and that sentence is held nowhere else.
- `level-decider:` 14 to 3, `liveness-subject:` 4 to 0, `seat-resume-driver:` 4 to 0, `agent-launch-gate:` 3 to 0, `worker-shape:` 13 to 8.

The red `check-worker-shape` on that branch is the `level-decider` lines going, not a separate fault nobody has looked at.

This isn't the test architecture. `tools/code-comment/strip.ts` keeps only what the forms list names and deletes the rest, and I ran its classifier over one specimen of each: `test-classification`, `predicate-derivation`, `level-decider`, `worker-shape`, `seat-resume-driver`, `agent-launch-gate` and `@guard` all come back `prose` — the class it deletes most freely, a step below even `candidate`. Only the two shapes already on the list survive. So the 54 you ruled on were one shape's worth of a hole that swallows every declaration we write for our own checks.

My recommendation is to hold that deploy until the strip refuses a comment it cannot show nothing parses, rather than deleting whatever the list does not happen to name. The test-lane question is real and worth your session — it just isn't what did this.

Filed at `pages/finding/code-comment/pragma-markers-name-no-declaration-of-ours.finding.md`.
